subject: math
title: Probability: Impossible, Unlikely, Equally Likely, Likely or Certain
seo_title: Grade 3 Probability Worksheets: Likely, Unlikely, Certain (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Use mathematical language, including the terms “impossible”, “unlikely”, “equally likely”, “likely”, and “certain”, to describe the likelihood of complementary events happening, and use that likelihood to make predictions and informed decisions
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on probability: describe events as impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely or certain, compare spinners and bags of counters, work with complementary events (red or not red) and make predictions from experiments. 100 questions with an answer key, following the Ontario curriculum (D2.1). Helpful EQAO practice.
key_big: The bigger the part of the spinner or bag, the more likely the outcome.
key_sub: Use the words impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely and certain. An event and its complement (red and not red) cover everything: if red is likely, not red is unlikely.
body_html:
The five probability words

Probability tells us how likely something is to happen. Impossible means it can never happen. Certain means it must happen. Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not. Likely means it will probably happen. Equally likely means it is just as likely to happen as not to happen.

WordMeaningExample
impossiblecan never happenA moose will fly over the school.
unlikelycould happen, but probably will notA black bear will walk into the classroom.
equally likelysame chance to happen or notA tossed coin will land on heads.
likelywill probably happenThere will be snow in Ottawa in January.
certainmust happenNext July 1 will be Canada Day.

Spinners: look at the size of each part

A spinner is more likely to land on a colour that covers more of it. Compare the size of the parts, not just the number of sections.

Example

Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?

Red is one big section: half of the spinner. The two blue sections together are less than half.

Answer: red

Bags of counters

When you pick without looking, the colour with more counters is more likely. The same number of each colour means they are equally likely.

Example

Is picking a blue counter unlikely or impossible?

There is 1 blue counter, so it could happen. It is not impossible.

Answer: unlikely

Red or not red: complementary events

The complement of an event is everything else that could happen. The complement of “landing on red” is “landing on not red”. One of the two always happens.

If red is …then not red is …
impossiblecertain
unlikelylikely
equally likelyequally likely
likelyunlikely
certainimpossible

Predictions and decisions

Use the chance to predict. A number cube has 6 faces, and each face is equally likely. If red is 1 of 4 equal sections, predict red about 1 time in every 4 spins. Real results vary a little each time.

Example

Kai wins if he picks red. Bag A: 3 red, 5 blue. Bag B: 5 red, 3 blue. Which bag should he choose?

Red is unlikely in Bag A and likely in Bag B.

Answer: Bag B

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Saying certain when it is only likelyCertain means it must happen every time. If it could fail, it is likely
Saying impossible when it is only unlikelyIf it could happen even once, it is not impossible
Counting sections, not their sizeCompare how much of the spinner each colour covers
Choosing your favourite colourLook at how much of the spinner or bag is that colour
Thinking the complement is just one other colourNot red means every colour that is not red
Thinking tails is due after many headsA coin does not remember: heads and tails stay equally likely

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about probability in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario Mathematics Curriculum (2020), expectation D2.1, Grade 3 students use the words impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely and certain to describe events and their complements, such as red and not red. They use these words to make predictions and informed decisions.
The complement of an event is everything else that could happen. The complement of landing on red is landing on not red, so if red is likely, not red is unlikely.

faq.q: What is the difference between unlikely and impossible?
faq.a: Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not, like picking the one blue counter from a bag of ten. Impossible means it can never happen, like rolling a 7 on a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6.

faq.q: Is probability on the Grade 3 EQAO math assessment?
faq.a: The Grade 3 EQAO math assessment is based on the Ontario curriculum, which includes data and probability. Practising the probability words with spinners, bags and number cubes is useful preparation.

sets.title: Everyday events: from impossible to certain

items.q: Next July 1 will be Canada Day. How likely is this?
items.e: Canada Day is on July 1 every year. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: Owen is 8 years old. On his next birthday, he will turn 9. How likely is this?
items.e: Everyone gets one year older on their birthday. 8 + 1 = 9, so it is certain.

items.q: Tomorrow is Friday. The day after tomorrow will be Saturday. How likely is this?
items.e: The days of the week always come in the same order. Saturday always comes after Friday, so it is certain.

items.q: Mei lets go of a hockey puck. It will fall down. How likely is this?
items.e: When you let go of a puck, it always falls. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: A moose will fly over the school like a bird. How likely is this?
items.e: Moose cannot fly. This can never happen, so it is impossible.

items.q: Liam is 8 years old. Next year he will be 7 years old. How likely is this?
items.e: You cannot get younger. Next year Liam will be 9, so being 7 is impossible.

items.q: A beaver will drive the school bus tomorrow. How likely is this?
items.e: A beaver cannot drive a bus. This can never happen, so it is impossible.

items.q: Which event is impossible?
c: Ava will lose a tooth this year
Nathan will see a Canada goose today
items.e: Every week has 7 days, so a week with 9 days can never happen. The other events could happen.

items.q: There will be snow on the ground in Ottawa on January 15. How likely is this?
items.e: Ottawa usually has snow on the ground in the middle of January. But a warm spell could melt it, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: A July afternoon in Toronto will be warm. How likely is this?
items.e: July is summer in Toronto, so most afternoons are warm. A few days can be cool and rainy, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: The next vehicle that drives past the school will have 4 wheels. How likely is this?
items.e: Most vehicles on the road are cars with 4 wheels. But the next one could be a motorcycle or a truck, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Students will go outside for recess on a sunny day in June. How likely is this?
items.e: On a sunny June day, students almost always go out for recess. Something could still change the plan, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Emma will find a $20 bill on the sidewalk on the way to school. How likely is this?
items.e: It could happen, but it almost never does. So it is unlikely. It is not impossible: people do drop money.

items.q: A black bear will walk into the classroom today. How likely is this?
items.e: Bears live in the forest. One could wander into a school, but it hardly ever happens. So it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: It will rain on every single day of July in Winnipeg. How likely is this?
items.e: Winnipeg has many sunny days in July. Rain on all 31 days could happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Jayden’s team will score 20 goals in one hockey game. How likely is this?
items.e: Hockey teams usually score a few goals in a game. 20 goals is possible, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Hana tosses a coin. It will land on heads. How likely is this?
items.e: A coin has 2 sides: heads and tails. Heads is as likely to happen as not to happen, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Mateo’s friend hides a toonie in one of her two closed hands. Mateo picks a hand. He will pick the hand with the toonie. How likely is this?
items.e: There are 2 hands and the toonie is in 1 of them. Picking the toonie hand and picking the empty hand have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: The teacher flips a coin to choose gym class or art first. Gym class will be first. How likely is this?
items.e: The coin has 2 sides, one for gym and one for art. Gym first and art first have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Only 3 of the 24 students will be picked to read the morning announcements. Chloe says, “It is impossible that I will be picked.” Which word should she use instead?
items.e: 3 of the 24 students will be picked, so Chloe could be one of them. It is possible, but not very likely. The right word is unlikely, not impossible.

sets.title: Spinners: look at the size of each part

items.q: The spinner has 4 equal sections. Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are red and only 1 is blue, so red is most likely. (There is no green, so green is impossible.)

items.q: The spinner has 6 equal sections. Which colour is the arrow least likely to land on?
items.e: Only 1 of the 6 equal sections is green. 5 are yellow. Green has the smallest part, so it is least likely.

items.q: Landing on red is …
items.e: Every section is red. The arrow must land on red, so it is certain.

items.q: Landing on red is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 6 equal sections is red. It can happen, but not often, so it is unlikely. It is not impossible, because there is a red section.

items.q: Landing on green is …
items.e: There is no green section on this spinner. The arrow can never land on green, so it is impossible.

items.q: Landing on green is …
items.e: 5 of the 6 equal sections are green, so green is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 purple section.

items.q: Landing on red is …
items.e: 2 of the 4 equal sections are red and 2 are not. Red covers half of the spinner, so landing on red and not landing on red are equally likely.

items.q: Landing on blue is …
items.e: The blue part covers 3 quarters of the spinner. The red part is only 1 quarter. So blue is likely, but not certain.

items.q: Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
items.e: Do not just count sections. Look at their size. The red part is half of the spinner. The two blue sections are small: together they are less than half.

items.q: Kai says blue is most likely, because blue has the most sections. Which colour is most likely?
items.e: Kai counted sections, not their size. The one yellow section is half of the whole spinner. Blue and red each cover only a quarter, so yellow is most likely.

items.q: Which colour can the arrow never land on?
items.e: The spinner has red, blue and yellow sections. There is no green, so green is impossible. Yellow has only 1 section, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Which sentence is true?
c: Red is more likely than blue
Red and blue are equally likely
items.e: Half of the spinner is red and half is blue. The parts are the same size, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Which colours are equally likely?
items.e: Each colour has 2 of the 6 equal sections. They all cover the same amount, so all three are equally likely.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on red impossible?
items.e: Spinner D has no red section, so red is impossible there. Spinner A has 1 red section: red is unlikely there, but not impossible.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on red most likely?
items.e: Compare how much of each spinner is red. C is three quarters red. D has 3 red sections, but they are small: together they are less than half of the spinner.

items.q: On which spinner are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: Spinner A is half red and half blue, so red and blue are equally likely. In C, red and blue each have 1 section, but the red section is bigger, so red is more likely there.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on blue certain?
items.e: Certain means it must happen. Only Spinner B is all blue. On A and C, blue is likely, but not certain, because there is another colour too.

items.q: Ethan colours a spinner with 4 equal sections. He wants landing on red to be unlikely, but not impossible. How many sections should he colour red?
items.e: 1 red section out of 4 makes red unlikely. 0 red sections would make red impossible. 3 would make it likely, and 4 would make it certain.

items.q: Sofia’s spinner has 8 equal sections. She colours 4 sections red and the rest blue. Which sentence is true?
c: Red and blue are equally likely
items.e: 8 − 4 = 4 sections are blue. 4 red and 4 blue sections of the same size cover the same amount, so red and blue are equally likely.

items.q: Zoe says the arrow will probably land on yellow, because yellow is her favourite colour. Which colour is the arrow more likely to land on?
items.e: Your favourite colour does not change the chance. 6 of the 8 equal sections are green and 2 are yellow, so green is more likely.

sets.title: Bags and cards: equally likely or not?

items.q: Amira picks one counter from the bag without looking. Which colour is she most likely to pick?
items.e: There are 6 red counters and only 2 blue counters. More red counters means red is more likely.

items.q: Noah picks one counter without looking. Which colour is he least likely to pick?
items.e: There is only 1 green counter and 7 yellow counters, so green is least likely.

items.q: Picking a blue counter from this bag is …
items.e: Every counter in the bag is blue, so you must pick blue. It is certain.

items.q: Picking a green counter from this bag is …
items.e: There are only red and yellow counters. There is no green counter, so it is impossible.

items.q: Picking a red counter from this bag is …
items.e: 7 of the 8 counters are red, so red is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 blue counter.

items.q: Picking a red counter from this bag is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 counters is red. It can happen, but not often, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Picking a red counter from this bag is …
items.e: 4 of the 8 counters are red and 4 are not. Picking red and not picking red have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Which two colours are equally likely to be picked?
items.e: There are 3 red, 3 blue and 2 yellow counters. Red and blue have the same number, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Put the colours in order from most likely to least likely.
items.e: Count each colour: yellow 5, red 2, green 1. The most counters is most likely: yellow, red, green.

items.q: Mei takes all the blue counters out of the bag. Now picking a red counter is …
items.e: After the blue counters come out, only the 3 red counters are left. You must pick red, so it is certain.

items.q: Kai puts 6 more green counters into the bag. Which colour is now more likely to be picked?
items.e: Green: 2 + 6 = 8 counters. Red: 6 counters. 8 is more than 6, so green is now more likely.

items.q: How many red counters must Zoe add to make red and blue equally likely?
items.e: Red and blue are equally likely when there are the same number of each. Blue has 5. Red has 2, so add 5 − 2 = 3 red counters.

items.q: Which bag makes picking a red counter certain?
items.e: Bag D has only red counters, so red is certain. Bag B is likely to give red, but not certain, because it has 1 blue counter.

items.q: From which bag is picking a yellow counter impossible?
items.e: Bag A has no yellow counters, so yellow is impossible. Bag B has 1 yellow counter, so yellow is unlikely there, not impossible.

items.q: From which bag is picking a blue counter most likely?
items.e: Each bag has 6 counters. Bag B has the most blue counters (5), so blue is most likely there.

items.q: From which bag are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: Bag C has 3 red and 3 blue counters. The same number of each colour means they are equally likely.

items.q: Leah has 10 hockey cards face down: 5 goalie cards and 5 player cards. She turns over one card. Which sentence is true?
c: A goalie card and a player card are equally likely
A goalie card is more likely
items.e: There are 5 goalie cards and 5 player cards. The same number of each means they are equally likely.

items.q: Amira’s bag has 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. She wants picking a blue counter to be impossible. What should she do?
items.e: Impossible means it can never happen. If there are no blue counters left, blue can never be picked. Adding red counters only makes blue unlikely.

items.q: A bag has 10 counters. Picking a red counter is certain. How many red counters are in the bag?
items.e: Certain means it must happen, so every counter must be red: all 10. With 9 red and 1 other counter, red is likely, not certain.

items.q: At the school fun fair, a prize box has 20 prizes: 15 pencils, 4 sticker sheets and 1 toy car. Olivia picks one prize without looking. Which prize is she least likely to get?
items.e: There is only 1 toy car out of 20 prizes, so it is least likely. 15 of the 20 prizes are pencils, so a pencil is most likely.

sets.title: Red or not red: complementary events

items.q: Landing on red is unlikely. Landing on a colour that is not red is …
items.e: Not red means blue here. 3 of the 4 equal sections are not red, so not red is likely. When red is unlikely, not red is likely.

items.q: Picking a red counter is likely. Picking a counter that is not red is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 8 counters is not red. It can happen, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Landing on a colour that is not blue is …
items.e: Not blue means red here. Red covers 2 of the 4 equal sections: half of the spinner. So not blue and blue are equally likely.

items.q: Picking a counter that is not green is …
items.e: Every counter is green. There is no counter that is not green, so it is impossible.

items.q: Picking a counter that is not red is …
items.e: There are no red counters in the bag. Every counter is not red, so picking a counter that is not red is certain.

items.q: Landing on red is likely. What can you say about not landing on red?
items.e: Red and not red cover the whole spinner together. If red covers the bigger part, not red covers the smaller part, so it is unlikely.

items.q: Picking a purple marble from a bag is impossible. Picking a marble that is not purple is …
items.e: There are no purple marbles, so every marble is not purple. You must pick one that is not purple. It is certain.

items.q: Rolling a 6 on a number cube is unlikely. Rolling a number that is not 6 is …
items.e: Not 6 means 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: 5 of the 6 faces. So it is likely. It is not certain, because you could roll a 6.

items.q: What is the complement of “the coin lands on heads”?
c: the coin lands on a number
the coin lands on heads again
the coin lands on heads or tails
items.e: The complement is everything else that could happen. A coin has only heads and tails, so the complement of heads is tails.

items.q: What is the complement of “landing on red”?
items.e: The complement is every outcome that is not red. On this spinner that is blue or yellow, not just one of them.

items.q: Landing on a colour that is not green is …
items.e: Red, blue and yellow are not green: 3 of the 4 equal sections. So it is likely. It is not certain, because there is a green section.

items.q: Owen rolls a number cube. Rolling an even number is …
items.e: Even numbers: 2, 4, 6 (3 faces). Not even: 1, 3, 5 (3 faces). 3 and 3 are the same, so even and not even are equally likely.

items.q: Priya rolls a number cube. Which is the complement of “rolling a 1”?
items.e: The complement is every other outcome: 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. Rolling a 1 is unlikely, so its complement is likely.

items.q: Landing on a colour that is not red is …
items.e: Not red means blue or yellow. Those two small parts together are only a quarter of the spinner. So not red is unlikely, but not impossible.

items.q: On which spinner are landing on red and landing on not red equally likely?
items.e: On Spinner B, red covers half of the spinner and not red covers the other half. So red and not red are equally likely there.

items.q: From which bag is picking a counter that is not blue certain?
items.e: Bag B has no blue counters, so every counter is not blue. That is certain. In Bag A, not blue is likely. In Bag C, it is impossible. In Bag D, it is equally likely.

items.q: In Owen’s bag, picking a red counter is certain. What about picking a counter that is not red?
items.e: Certain means every counter is red. Then there is no counter that is not red, so it is impossible.

items.q: The weather forecast says rain in Halifax tomorrow is likely. “It will not rain in Halifax tomorrow” is …
items.e: Rain and no rain are complements. If rain is likely, no rain is unlikely. It is not impossible: forecasts can be wrong.

items.q: Olivia says, “Landing on red is unlikely, so landing on not red is impossible.” Is she right?
c: No, not red is also unlikely
items.e: Red is unlikely, but it can happen. So not red does not always happen: it is likely, not certain or impossible.

items.q: Which is more likely: picking blue or picking not blue?
items.e: Blue: 4 counters. Not blue: red and yellow, 2 + 2 = 4 counters. 4 and 4 are the same, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Which colour came up most often?
c: they all came up the same
items.e: Red: 1 group of 5 and 4 more = 9. Blue: 7. Yellow: 4. Red has the most tally marks.

items.q: How many times did Maya spin altogether?
items.e: Add the tallies: 9 + 7 + 4 = 20.

items.q: How many more times did red come up than yellow?
items.e: Red 9, yellow 4. How many more means subtract: 9 − 4 = 5.

items.q: Lucas spins this spinner 20 times. Which result would be most surprising?
items.e: Half the spinner is red and half is blue, so you expect about 10 of each. Results near 10 are normal. Red every single time is possible, but very unlikely.

items.q: Benjamin spins this spinner 20 times. Which prediction is best?
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are blue, so blue should come up about 3 times as often as red. Blue 15 and red 5 fits best. The results can change a little each time.

items.q: Hana spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should she predict red?
items.e: Red is 1 of 4 equal sections, so about 1 spin in every 4 is red. 40 ÷ 4 = 10. 30 is the prediction for blue, not red.

items.q: Nathan rolled a number cube 30 times. Which number did he roll most often?
items.e: Find the biggest number in the Times row: 7. That is under the number 5. (6 is the biggest number on the cube, not the most rolled.)

items.q: Nathan says 5 is the easiest number to roll, because it came up most. Is he right?
c: No, 4 is the easiest to roll
No, each number is equally likely
No, 6 is the easiest to roll
Yes, 5 will come up most every time
items.e: Each face of a number cube has the same chance. Results vary: next time a different number may come up most.

items.q: Benjamin picks a counter from a bag, looks at it and puts it back. He does this 20 times. He gets red 17 times and blue 3 times. Which bag did he most likely use?
items.e: Red came up much more often than blue, so the bag probably has many more red counters. It cannot be 10 red and 0 blue, because then blue would be impossible, and he picked blue 3 times.

items.q: Ava’s spinner has 4 equal sections. Which spinner did she most likely use?
items.e: Green came up 14 times and purple 6 times. Green came up much more often, so green probably covers more of the spinner. With 4 purple sections, green would be impossible.

items.q: Arjun tosses a coin 4 times and gets heads every time. What about the next toss?
c: Heads and tails are still equally likely
items.e: A coin does not remember what happened before. Every toss, heads and tails are equally likely.

items.q: Kai wins a prize if he picks a red counter. Bag A has 3 red and 5 blue counters. Bag B has 5 red and 3 blue counters. Which bag should he choose?
c: Either bag, they are the same
items.e: Both bags have 8 counters. Bag B has 5 red, Bag A has only 3. Red is likely in Bag B, so Bag B is the better choice.

items.q: Zoe and Jayden play a game. Zoe gets a point when the spinner lands on red. Jayden gets a point when it lands on blue. Which spinner makes the game fair?
items.e: A game is fair when both players are equally likely to win. With 2 equal red and 2 equal blue sections, red and blue are equally likely.

items.q: Liam’s class spins a spinner 50 times. They get blue 38 times and yellow 12 times. What is the best prediction for the next spin?
c: Yellow is more likely, because it is due
items.e: Blue came up much more often, so blue probably covers more of the spinner. Blue is more likely, but not certain. Yellow is never “due”.

items.q: At the school winter carnival, 100 raffle tickets are sold. Ava buys 1 ticket. Ava winning the raffle is …
items.e: Ava has only 1 of the 100 tickets. She could win, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Ethan’s family buys 95 of the 100 raffle tickets. Ethan’s family winning the raffle is …
items.e: 95 of the 100 tickets are theirs, so it is likely. It is not certain, because 5 tickets belong to other people.

items.q: A box has 20 granola bars: 15 chocolate chip and 5 oatmeal. Leah takes one without looking. Getting an oatmeal bar is …
items.e: Only 5 of the 20 bars are oatmeal, and 15 are chocolate chip. Oatmeal can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Sofia’s class has 24 students. Each student puts their name in a toque, and the teacher picks one. Picking the name of a student in Sofia’s class is …
items.e: Every name in the toque belongs to a student in the class, so it is certain.

items.q: Owen rolls a number cube 12 times. He gets a 6 three times. How many times did he not get a 6?
items.e: Not a 6 means all the other rolls: 12 − 3 = 9.

items.q: Chloe spins a spinner 20 times. She gets red 8 times, blue 5 times and yellow the rest of the time. How many times did she get yellow?
items.e: Step 1: red and blue: 8 + 5 = 13. Step 2: 20 − 13 = 7 times yellow.
